food.text: Sausage-making in German lands was regulated early. Rules on what may go into sausages have been in force in Germany since the 13th century, and the market ordinance of Landshut in 1236 set down that only top-quality meat could be made into sausages.

In the Late Middle Ages, moonshine production picked up, especially in German-speaking regions. By the 13th century, Hausbrand, literally 'home-burnt' from gebrannter wein (distilled wine), was commonplace, marking the origin of brandy.

The aromatic herb tarragon was brought to Transylvania by the Transylvanian Saxons during the Middle Ages. These German settlers had lived in Transylvania since the mid-12th century, and marjoram is another important herb in their traditional cuisine.
Nürnberger Bratwurst was first mentioned in a document in 1313. In it, the council of Nuremberg described the recipe as a special product.

By the end of the Late Middle Ages, spirits were so ingrained among ordinary people that restrictions on sales and production began to appear in the late 15th century. In 1496, the city of Nuremberg restricted the selling of aquavit on Sundays and official holidays.
The origin of pierogi is unknown and debated. One theory holds that in the 13th century Saint Hyacinth of Poland brought these filled dumplings from the Far East via what was then the Kievan Rus'.

art.text: Martin Schongauer worked in Alsace in the last part of the 15th century and was the culmination of late Gothic German painting. His style was sophisticated and harmonious, and he increasingly made engravings, whose prints were known in Italy and other countries.

The Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire is a hoop crown with a characteristic octagonal shape, made of eight hinged golden plates. The earliest known mention of it dates from the 12th century. It is now kept in the Imperial Treasury at the Hofburg in Vienna.
art.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

art.text: The Church of St. Michael in Hildesheim was commissioned by Bishop Bernward, with construction starting in 1010 and finishing by 1033, after his death. It is one of the best preserved examples of Ottonian architecture and became famous for housing a number of artworks and reliquaries.

The Kammerzell House in Strasbourg was built in 1427 and transformed in 1467 and again in 1589. It is one of the most ornate and well-preserved medieval civil housing buildings in late-Gothic architecture in areas once belonging to the Holy Roman Empire, in the Rhineland black and white timber-framed style.

Around 1260, a group of sandstone figures was created in the choir of Meissen Cathedral. The most famous representation of Adelaide in German art belongs to this group. She is shown beside her husband, who was not canonized, because he founded the diocese of Meissen with her.

Historians disagree about when the Imperial Crown was made. Some date it to the second half of the tenth century, but John B. Freed argues its inscriptions are no earlier than the second half of the eleventh century. He proposes it was made for Conrad III, citing the title on the crown, which matches how Conrad was styled in a 1142 letter, and says the plaque of the ailing King Hezekiah fits Conrad, who had become seriously ill with tertian malaria during the Second Crusade. Conrad was ultimately never crowned as emperor.
art.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

art.text: Over one hundred Romanesque buildings survive in Poland, and the style was influenced by Cologne, especially early on. Examples include the Crypt of Saint Leonard at Wawel Hill in Kraków and the Cathedral of Płock, built in 1144.

The bronze Gniezno Doors, made around 1175, are recognized as the first major work of Polish art with a national theme. Their relief shows eighteen scenes from the life and death of Saint Adalbert. They are an important example of Romanesque art.

In 1349, Charles IV took the Imperial Regalia, which includes the Imperial Crown, to Karlstein Castle near Prague. He had just built the castle for that purpose. An inventory he ordered in 1350 is the last mention of an item that was removed from the crown.
art.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

art.text: Mainz Cathedral, also called the Cathedral of St. Martin, suffered severe fire damage on the day of its consecration in 1009. It was rebuilt by 1036 but burnt down again in 1081. Only a few Ottonian features survive, such as the lower floors of the circular staircases of the towers.
German conservatism in painting is shown by the late use of gold backgrounds. Many artists were still using them well into the 15th century.
The brick Church of St. Jacob in Sandomierz was founded in 1226 by Iwo Odrowąż and built by his nephew, St. Jacek Odrowąż. Its campanile, however, was built in early Gothic style in the 14th century.

Medieval architecture was described as both an art and a science of designing and constructing buildings. In North Germany and around the Baltic, builders made the Brick Gothic style widespread. Gothic buildings there used features such as pointed arches, rib vaulting and exterior buttresses.

Since the 14th century, Adelaide has also been given a model church or a ship as an attribute in art. The ship refers to the vessel by which she is said to have escaped from captivity. She had been imprisoned for four months at Garda after refusing to marry Adalbert, the son of Berengar II of Italy, who had tried to force the marriage to cement his own power. She is usually shown in the garb of an empress, with sceptre and crown.

In 1424, with Bohemia suffering the troubles of the Hussite Wars, Sigismund moved the Imperial Regalia to Visegrád and then to Nuremberg. There they were permanently kept in the Heilig-Geist-Spital, except during coronations, which were held in Aachen until 1531.
art.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: The Reichsfahne, or imperial flag, was the sign of the united armed forces of the Holy Roman Empire until the late 15th century. In the 12th century it apparently showed a white cross on a red field. The king could also send it to local lords to sanction them in their defense of Landfrieden.
war.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: Between 1440 and 1460 the nobles defeated the cities and peasants in a series of Cities Wars. They then began aggressively raising rents and tightened the bonds of serfdom, restricting access to the commons where peasants pastured their livestock. The article says that when a peasant died, the lord was entitled to his best cattle, garments and tools, and a peasant needed the lord's permission, and had to pay a tax, to marry.

In 1310 the Luxembourg King Henry VII of Germany crossed the Alps with 5,000 men and moved into Milan. He had himself crowned king of Italy with a mock-up of the Iron Crown, which sparked a Guelph rebellion under Lord Guido della Torre. Henry then restored the rule of Matteo I Visconti.
In 1415 King Sigismund gave the imperial banner to the Swiss Confederacy. This sanctioned their war against the Habsburgs, showing how the flag could grant legitimacy to a local fight.
war.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: When the Holy Roman Empire took part in the Crusades, a war flag was flown alongside the black-gold imperial banner. Known as the Saint George Flag, it was a white cross on a red background, the reverse of the St George's Cross used as the flag of Lombardy and England.
war.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: In 1245 Pope Innocent IV deposed Emperor Frederick II, and Henry Raspe, Landgrave of Thuringia, was set up as anti-king to Frederick's son Conrad IV. The deposition was widely regarded as illegitimate, and no monarch in Europe offered meaningful support for Innocent's crusade against the emperor. Henry Raspe was killed in 1247.
An early bearer of the Reichsfahne was Werner I, count of Winterthur, who carried the flag for Conrad II and Henry III. He was killed in the battle at Brůdek in 1040.
war.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: Throughout 1249 and 1250 Conrad IV steadily defeated the anti-king William of Holland, whose power never extended beyond a tenuous hold north of the Rhine. Conrad also extracted a truce from the major ecclesiastical princes. He died of malaria near Rome in 1254 while consolidating his Sicilian inheritance.
The Reichssturmfahne, the Imperial War Flag, was granted to Ulrich III, Count of Württemberg, in 1336. It remained part of the House of Württemberg's heraldic insignia until the 19th century.
war.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: Historian John B. Freed notes that Conrad III became seriously ill during the Second Crusade, suffering from tertian malaria. It hindered him from carrying out his responsibilities from the end of August 1149 until April 1150, and Freed links it to the making of the Imperial Crown.
war.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

literature.text: Medieval German literature is usually split into two main periods. Old High German literature (750 to 1050) came from the monasteries and was almost entirely religious. Middle High German literature (1050 to 1350) came from the noble courts and focused on knightly exploits and courtly love.

The Middle High German period is conventionally taken to end in 1350. Early New High German begins after the invention of movable type in the mid-15th century. Literature from the late 14th and early 15th century falls in the cracks between the two and can be classified as either.

The Germanic Nibelungenlied began as an oral tale about events of the distant past, set in the 6th century. Its surviving manuscripts date only from the 13th century, centuries after the events it recounts.

Works from the transitional period between Middle and New High German include The Ring (c. 1410) and the poems of Oswald von Wolkenstein and Johannes von Tepl. Along with these, the German versions of Pontus and Sidonia are also listed among them.

In the early 11th century, Notker III produced extensive works continuing the long tradition of translating and adapting Latin Christian texts into Old High German. His writing was part of a scholarly effort that had begun with translation aids for people learning to read Latin.

Sebastian Brant's Ship of Fools (1494) and the works of Hans Folz are arguably part of the transitional period between Middle and New High German. They come from the late years of the medieval German literary tradition.

After Notker, there is a gap of some 40 years in the written record. Then evidence appears of a new tradition of biblical verse in Early Middle High German. This was followed by the flourishing secular literature of Middle High German.

The Imperial Crown can only be dated back to the 13th century, when it is described in a medieval poem. The poem mentions the Waise (the Orphan) stone, a prominent jewel on the front of the crown. The first definite picture of the crown is a later mural in Karlstein Castle near Prague.
literature.source_title: Imperial Regalia of the Holy Roman Empire

literature.text: The Volksbuch, or chapbook, tradition would flourish in the 16th century. Its origin lies in the second half of the 15th century, in the transitional years of German literature after movable type arrived.

science.text: Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1400–1468) invented the printing press with movable types and an oil-based ink in the Free City of Mainz. From there the technique began to spread across the world. In time it created the conditions for scientific publications to become generally accessible.

Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a polymath who worked as a philosopher, lawyer, natural scientist and theologian. He was also a Dominican and became Bishop of Regensburg. His wide learning made him one of the most prominent scholars of medieval German lands.

In 1365 Duke Rudolf IV founded the University of Vienna, which is the oldest university in the German-speaking world. Its foundation deed already provided for a public library where books left by deceased members of the university would be collected. By the mid-15th century it was home to more than 6,000 students.

Hildegard of Bingen, a German Benedictine abbess, wrote on botany and medicine as well as theology and music. Her Causae et Curae gave specific instructions for bleeding patients, including how much blood to take, "the amount that a thirsty person can swallow in one gulp". It also told readers to check a patient's blood, pulse, urine and stool, and showed how to bleed animals. A number of scholars have considered her the founder of scientific natural history in Germany.

Georg von Peuerbach became known for a streamlined presentation of Ptolemaic astronomy in his Theoricae Novae Planetarum. He enrolled at the University of Vienna in 1446 and studied mathematics there, even though the university had no professors of astronomy at the time.

Albertus Magnus earned the name Magnus, meaning "the Great", because his knowledge was so great and so diverse. He was also given the title of Doctor of the Church and the honorary title of doctor universalis.

In 1460 Cardinal Bessarion asked Peuerbach and Regiomontanus to prepare a shorter, clearer version of Ptolemy's Almagest as a teaching text. Peuerbach had finished six volumes when he died in 1461. Regiomontanus completed it, and the 13-volume Epitome of the Almagest was published in 1496.

Regiomontanus moved to Nuremberg in 1471 and worked there with the merchant Bernhard Walther. He founded the world's first scientific printing press, and in 1472 published the first printed astronomical textbook, Peuerbach's Theoricae novae Planetarum.

Gutenberg's contributions to printing included oil-based ink, adjustable molds and a wooden press similar to the agricultural screw presses of the period. His type metal was a mixture of lead, tin and antimony that melted at a low temperature, cast well and made durable type.

Nicholas of Cusa wrote on philosophy and theology and came from Kues, Germany. In his book On Learned Ignorance, finished in 1440, he argued that mankind cannot grasp the infinity of God through rational knowledge, so the limits of science must be passed by means of speculation.

Bessarion considered George of Trebizond's new Latin translation of the Almagest inaccurate and badly translated. Peuerbach's Greek was not good enough to make a new translation, but he knew the Almagest intimately. So he began a modernised, improved abridgement instead, and on his deathbed made Regiomontanus promise to finish it.

The Epitome of the Almagest became an important reference for Nicolaus Copernicus when he wrote De Revolutionibus. Regiomontanus carried the project on after Peuerbach's death, and it was published in 1496, twenty years after his own death in 1476.

The medical faculty of the University of Vienna, founded in 1365, was widely renowned in medieval times as an authority in medicine. Faculty records from as far back as 1399 show it mediating in disputes between barber surgeons, midwives and local landowners.

When Heidelberg University was founded in 1386, it was modelled on the University of Paris and included four faculties: philosophy, theology, jurisprudence and medicine. Marsilius of Inghen was elected its first rector, and by March 1390 it had 185 students.

Regiomontanus is shown holding an astrolabe in Hartmann Schedel's 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle. The chronicle contains thirteen illustrations of comets, but they are stylized rather than showing the actual objects.

politics.text: By the 13th century the Holy Roman Emperor was chosen by prince-electors rather than passing by inheritance. The Golden Bull of 1356 finally settled disputes among the electors. It named seven: the Archbishops of Mainz, Trier and Cologne, the King of Bohemia, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Duke of Saxony, and the Margrave of Brandenburg.

After Conrad IV, Frederick II's son, died in 1254, no king could win universal recognition during the Interregnum. The princes used the chance to consolidate their holdings and became even more independent as rulers. Rudolf I, a minor count, was eventually elected in 1273 as the first Habsburg to hold a royal title.

The Holy Roman Empire was politically decentralized, and for the first half of its history it was ruled by a travelling court. Kings and emperors toured between imperial palaces called Kaiserpfalzes, staying weeks or months and handling local legal matters, law and administration. Under the Habsburgs, Prague served as a favoured seat from 1355 to 1437.

The Holy Roman Empire had long periods with no emperor. One lasted 62 years, from 1250 to 1312, and another 55 years, from 1378 to 1433. With no central government, the article says feuding among the lesser nobility increased, leading to conflicts such as the Thuringian Counts' War and a general state of near-anarchy in Germany, where robber barons acted unopposed by the nominal system of justice. The crisis of government lasted throughout the late medieval period and ended only with the rise of the Habsburgs.

In 1338 the Declaration of Rhense established that election by a majority of the electors automatically conferred the royal title and rule over the empire. This meant no papal confirmation was needed. It marked a shift of power away from the papacy.

In the year 1000, Otto III made a pilgrimage to the Congress of Gniezno in Poland. There he established the Archdiocese of Gniezno and confirmed the royal status of the Piast ruler Bolesław I the Brave. Otto was expelled from Rome in 1001 and died at age 21 the next year.

In 1349 Charles IV took the Imperial Regalia to Karlstein Castle near Prague, which he had just built for that purpose. In 1424, with Bohemia troubled by the Hussite Wars, Sigismund moved them to Visegrád and then to Nuremberg. There they were kept permanently in the Heilig-Geist-Spital, except during coronations.
politics.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: In 1415 King Sigismund gave the imperial war banner to the Swiss Confederacy. This sanctioned their war against the Habsburgs. Such a banner could be sent by the king to local lords to sanction their defense of Landfrieden.
politics.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: In 1433 Sigismund of Luxemburg adopted the double-headed eagle as the imperial arms. Before that, the imperial eagle was usually single-headed. From then on the double-headed eagle served as the symbol of the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation.

King Rudolph III of Burgundy died without heirs on 2 February 1032, and Conrad II successfully claimed the kingship of Burgundy as well. He based the claim on an inheritance that Emperor Henry II had extorted from Rudolph in 1006. When Rudolph attempted to renounce that inheritance in 1016, Henry II invaded the Kingdom of Burgundy to enforce his claim.

philosophy.text: Albert the Great, a Dominican friar who lived from about 1200 to 1280, is described as the most eminent German Scholastic. He taught Aristotle's Physics and Nicomachean Ethics at Paris and Cologne.

Hildegard von Bingen (c. 1098–1179), a Neoplatonist nun and polymath, was called the "Sibyl of the Rhine". She wrote on theology, cosmology and natural philosophy. In her work Scivias (1151), she wrote that God infused life with greenness.

Marsilius of Inghen, a student of Albert of Saxony, became the first rector at the third German university, the University of Heidelberg, founded in 1386. Before this, Albert of Saxony had been followed at Vienna by other thinkers.
Meister Eckhart was condemned for heresy after his death, and Henry Suso (1295–1366) defended him. Eckhart influenced the Friends of God and the priest John of Ruusbroec (1294–1381).

At St. Emmeram's in Regensburg, Otloh of Sankt Emmeram (c. 1010–c. 1072) and Manegold of Lautenbach (c. 1030–c. 1103) were sophisticated opponents of philosophy. By the twelfth century, all the monks at St. Emmeram's were illiterate.

Albert the Great's students included the Neoplatonist Theodoric of Freiberg (c. 1250–c. 1311), Thomas Aquinas, and the Aristotle translator William of Moerbeke (c. 1225–c. 1286). His teaching at Cologne and Paris thus shaped several later thinkers.
Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464) was a major figure of Northern Renaissance and German Renaissance humanism. He stood alongside Conrad Celtis (1459–1508) and the realist Johann Heynlin (c. 1425–1496).
John of Ruusbroec influenced the Brethren of the Common Life and Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471), a proponent of Devotio Moderna. Thomas à Kempis wrote The Imitation of Christ.
Berthold of Moosburg (d. c. 1365) succeeded Meister Eckhart at Cologne. He influenced Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361) and Heymeric de Campo (1395–1460).
Henry of Langenstein (c. 1325–1397) and Henry of Oyta (c. 1330–1397) followed Albert of Saxony at the University of Vienna. Langenstein taught Ockham's conciliar theory.
The Dominican school at Cologne was converted to a studium generale around 1388, making it the fourth German university. Later, Lambertus de Monte (c. 1430–1499) worked there as a Thomist.

culture.text: As Poland became Christian, the older pagan Slavic mythology-based culture gave way to a new Christian culture under the Piast dynasty. Around the 12th century the church network in Poland consisted of about one thousand parishes grouped in eight dioceses.

A warrior nobility dominated feudal German society in the Middle Ages, while most Germans were peasants with few political rights. The church also played an important role in the Holy Roman Empire and competed with the nobility for power.

From the 11th century Germans moved eastwards in a movement known as the Ostsiedlung. From the 12th century German speakers settled as merchants and craftsmen in the Kingdom of Poland. They became a significant proportion of the population in many towns, such as Gdańsk.
Polish scholarship reached beyond Poland in the Middle Ages. Works discussed in Western Europe included a chronicle of popes and emperors by Martinus Polonus and the treatise on optics by Witelo.
Cracow Academy's faculties of astronomy, law and theology were staffed with prominent scholars. Stanisław of Skalbmierz, Paweł Włodkowic, Jan of Głogów and Wojciech of Brudzew were among them.

A growing sense of national identity in the late eleventh century made the term "Kingdom of the Germans" more popular in Germany. By the twelfth century, the historian Otto of Freising had to explain that East Francia was "now called the Kingdom of the Germans".
Charlemagne was canonised in December 1165 and January 1166. During the celebrations Frederick Barbarossa called Aachen the "head and seat of the German Kingdom".
